claims.text: Solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn exhibits dynamic mechanical behavior governed by the relative activation of deformation twinning and dislocation glide.
Higher strain rates promote deformation twinning in equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
Lower temperatures reduce stacking-fault energy in equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
Lower stacking-fault energy favors deformation twinning.
Deformation twinning enhances work hardening and helps maintain the strength–ductility balance.
At lower strain rates or elevated temperatures, dislocation glide dominates and twin formation is reduced.
Twin density and distribution relative to dislocation structures are the primary microstructural mediator of the dynamic response.
Deformation twins provide additional barriers to dislocation motion.
Twin-induced barriers to dislocation motion increase strain hardening and improve dynamic mechanical performance.
Higher temperatures increase dislocation mobility in equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
Increased dislocation mobility limits twin formation and reduces strain hardening.
Increasing strain rate at low temperature will measurably increase twin density.
The low-temperature, increased-strain-rate condition will exhibit greater work-hardening rate and dynamic strength than quasi-static room-temperature testing.
High-temperature or low-speed testing will produce lower twin densities correlated with reduced dynamic strain hardening.
A quasi-static, room-temperature strength–ductility balance has been reported for as-solidified, homogenized FeNiCrMn.
The proposed mechanism applies to cast, homogenized, equiatomic FeNiCrMn with controlled microstructure.
The proposed mechanism may not apply after substantial grain-size changes, cold working, or other processing that produces high defect densities or different microstructures.
Dynamic deformation twinning is a known mechanism in related high- and medium-entropy alloys.
The onset conditions and quantitative influence of dynamic twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn are uncertain.
